newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to ditch five-day bank opening limit.
newsitem.headline: France to ditch five-day bank opening limit.

text.p: The French government will revise a 60-year-old decree to allow banks to stay open six days a week instead of five, Labour Minister Jacques Barrot said on Tuesday.

Barrot told a news conference that banks and unions had failed to reach agreement on the issue and that the government would go ahead with plans to repeal the 1937 banking hours decree to allow bank branches stay open from Monday to Saturday.
The announcement drew an angry response from a common front of banking unions, which vowed to step up its protests against the move.

"If the decree passes tomorrow, we plan to take more radical action. We will launch protests aimed at disrupting the functioning of banks," said Pierre Gendre, a spokesman for the Force Ouvriere banking union.
The unions said they might also seek to snarl traffic on highways or block railway tracks.
But after a relatively low turnout for a strike last Friday against the proposed changes to banking hours, the unions stopped short of calling another walkout.
Unions called a one-day strike on Friday on the government was preparing to change banking hours regulation without sufficient negotiations.
Barrot said he would propose a new decree to the cabinet meeting on Wednesday and that it would allow banks to open from 7.30 a.m. to 8.30 p.m. each day, ending the current eight-hour limit.
"The 1937 decree belongs to an era, that of 1937," he said. "People need to be able to go to the bank on Saturday."

Barrot said the original proposals for the 1997 decree had been modified after consultation and that they now contained an obligation on banks to convene a works council meeting if changes in opening hours had not won employee approval.
Sunday would remain a "rest day" for all banks and staff would still be guaranteed a two-day break each week, he said.
But it could now be a Sunday-Monday break rather than a Saturday-Sunday break, he added.

Barrot said that the French commercial banking association (AFB) had agreed that the new decree would be put in to practice gradually and that the association believed the greater flexibility could preserve about 9,000 jobs that would otherwise have been at risk.
Some French banks have been able to open on Saturday's because of their special status but the aim is to generalise this to commercial banks which have been unable to do so.
